stories.title: Arc Raiders tests a pure PvE mode as player counts rebound
paragraphs: Embark is testing a pure player-versus-environment matchmaking option in Arc Raiders from October 13–20. The extraction shooter originally began as a PvE concept before shifting to a mix of player combat and AI enemies.

Executive producer Aleksander Grøndal told GamesRadar the test will help the studio judge player feedback and data; he said a separate PvE experience is possible, but no permanent split has been announced.

The test follows a Steam peak of 185,443 concurrent players after the October 8 Frozen Trail update, a seven-month high. The update and free trial helped drive the spike, and that Steam figure does not show whether interest will last or how console activity changed.

scoreNotes.general: A large return in Steam activity coincides with a test that could alter the game's PvPvE design, though durability and demand outside Steam remain unknown.
scoreNotes.heat: Steam concurrency reached 185,443, the highest since March, and the limited PvE test addresses a long-standing player request. This is a strong game-specific signal, not a platform-wide measure.
scoreNotes.time: The Frozen Trail audience peak came during the preceding week. Embark's PvE test runs October 13–20, making the experiment the latest meaningful development.
scoreNotes.ethos: GamesRadar reports SteamDB's peak and quotes executive producer Aleksander Grøndal on the test and possible design trade-offs. Steam data excludes console players, and the studio has not committed to a permanent mode.

nearMisses.title: YouTube clarifies monetization eligibility for some public-interest content
nearMisses.reason: YouTube's official page confirms an October guideline update, but gives no exact publication date, affected creator count, or evidence of creator response. The change is relevant, yet its scale and practical impact are too unclear for a main story.

scoreNotes.general: A verified policy clarification with uncertain timing and no evidence yet of how creators are affected.
scoreNotes.heat: The eligibility change could matter to creators covering public-interest issues, but no affected-channel count or audience discussion was found.
scoreNotes.time: YouTube labels the change October 2026 but does not give a day, so its fit within this update's window cannot be established.
scoreNotes.ethos: YouTube's own Help page states the policy clarification; its scope and timing are directly documented, while implementation effects are not.

paragraphs: YouTube's October 2026 advertiser-guideline update says some content of public interest, including coverage of congressional proceedings and debates over ongoing government actions, will be eligible to earn ad revenue under its Hateful and Derogatory Content and Harmful Acts and Unreliable Content policies.
The official page does not give an exact update date or explain how many videos or creators may be affected. No independent creator response or measurable impact surfaced in this search.
